title: Challenging Consensus, Scientist Says Epstein Autopsy Photos Show Homicide
summary: Investigations have found most evidence in Jeffrey Epstein’s death points to suicide. Michael Freeman, a forensic scientist who studies homicides, got rare access to the autopsy file and disagrees.

Michael Freeman says he had one thought when he first saw a photo from Jeffrey Epstein’s autopsy: “Wait a minute, that doesn’t look like a hanging mark.”


The noose had not left a smooth, consistent line on Mr. Epstein’s neck that slanted to a peak, as in a textbook hanging. Instead, the mark was deep, ragged and branched into a Y-shape on one side.


Dr. Freeman, a forensic scientist who studies bias and error in death investigations, spent a year examining Mr. Epstein’s autopsy file, which was given to him by the dead man’s brother.


He is seeking to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal, but has been rejected so far. On Monday he presented them at the Middle Temple, a London legal society, where he argued that Mr. Epstein’s injuries are most plausibly explained by homicidal strangulation. He also asserted that injuries on the body suggest there was a struggle, contrary to the medical examiner’s findings.


“The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” he said.


The totality of the circumstances surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death in a federal detention center in 2019 points[overwhelmingly to suicide](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/06/16/magazine/jeffrey-epstein-death-final-days.html) , and several investigations have failed to produce evidence that anyone other than Mr. Epstein had a hand in it. Dr. Freeman’s analysis, parts of which he floated in a[New York Times investigation earlier this year](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/06/16/magazine/jeffrey-epstein-death-final-days.html) , may rekindle long-smoldering debates about his death.
